title: Stress-Induced Oculogyric Crisis in Septo-Optic Dysplasia: Case Report
case_prompt:
A 27-year-old white woman with congenital septo-optic dysplasia presented with acute, recurrent, painless, bilateral, simultaneous, intermittent, stereotyped tonic conjugate upward deviation of her eyes. The episodes began after a stressful social encounter and increased in frequency and duration over months, occurring 2–3 times per week and lasting minutes to hours. She remained fully conscious with intact sphincter function and had no observed seizure activity. Occasionally the eye deviations were accompanied by dystonic body posturing. She denied bradykinesia, autonomic symptoms, or orolingual dyskinesias.

Her past history was significant for intrauterine brain hypoxia secondary to maternal diabetes and cocaine use, and she had stable hypopituitarism managed with hormone replacement. She also had migraine without aura. Current medications included levothyroxine, clonazepam, estradiol, hydrocortisone, metoprolol, nitroglycerin, and progesterone.

Brain MRI demonstrated a stable middle cranial fossa arachnoid cyst without hydrocephalus, pituitary hypoplasia, absence of the olfactory bulb, tuber cinereum, and anterior commissure, and optic nerve hypoplasia. EEG was normal. Endocrinologic studies showed a TSH of 0.01 mIU/L (consistent with levothyroxine therapy) and normal cortisol and estrogen levels on replacement.

On neuro-ophthalmologic examination, visual acuity was count-fingers at 3 ft in the right eye and 20/400 in the left eye, unchanged from baseline. She had pendular congenital nystagmus with roving eye movements, mild impairment of abduction and adduction in both eyes, and constricted visual fields (10° right, 30° left). Pupils were isochoric and poorly reactive. Anterior segments were unremarkable. Dilated fundus examination showed small optic nerves bilaterally with a cup-to-disk ratio of 0.7 and a flat hyperpigmented lesion on the left optic disc.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Consideration of versive seizures due to paroxysmal eye deviation — “Electroencephalography was normal, and she had no seizure clinically.”  
2. Consideration of paroxysmal tonic upward gaze as a mimic of sustained upward eye posturing — “the differential diagnoses of OGC include versive seizures, paroxysmal tonic upward gaze, encephalopathy, and ocular dyskinesias or tics.”  
3. Consideration of medication-induced ocular dystonia given known drug associations — “Although OGC is often a side effect of medications (e.g., antiemetics, neuroleptics, antipsychotics, anticonvulsants, and antidepressants)” and exclusion because “She was not taking any drugs reported in the literature to be related to OGC episodes.”  
4. Consideration of encephalopathy or other acute central causes — “the differential diagnoses of OGC include versive seizures, paroxysmal tonic upward gaze, encephalopathy, and ocular dyskinesias or tics,” with stable MRI and preserved consciousness arguing against encephalopathy.  
5. Consideration of ocular dyskinesias or tics as movement disorder mimics — “the differential diagnoses of OGC include versive seizures, paroxysmal tonic upward gaze, encephalopathy, and ocular dyskinesias or tics,” distinguished by the stereotyped tonic nature and duration of episodes.
